opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way we thought about it was really pretty simple. We had this technology, these large language models, that we'd been working on for years, and it was clear they were getting incredibly capable. The question was: what's the fastest way to get this into the hands of billions of people and let them figure out what it's good for?

What we didn't want was to build one narrow application and say, "This is what AI is for." Nobody really knows yet what all the use cases are. So the idea was to make something as general and flexible as possible, where users themselves create the characters and decide what they want to do with them. Some people want a study buddy, some want to practice a language, some want someone to talk through their day with, some want to play a game or tell a story together. If you let people define that, you get to see what's actually valuable instead of guessing.

There was also a practical side. These models aren't perfect; they make things up sometimes. If you put that in a setting where people expect perfectly accurate facts, that's a problem. But in entertainment and companionship, a bit of creativity is actually a feature. So it made sense to launch where the technology was already good enough to be really useful and fun, and then improve from there.

And I think a big part of it was just believing in the trajectory. The models are going to keep getting better, and a flexible, open-ended product lets you ride that curve. You aren't locked into one thing. As the intelligence improves, the product improves along with it, and users keep discovering new things to do with it.

r001.rationale: It says they wanted to get the technology to billions of people so users could discover what it was good for, rather than choosing one narrow use case.

r002.rationale: It explains that models sometimes make things up and that creativity is a feature in entertainment and companionship, making those settings a good fit.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, we didn't start with a very specific product thesis. When Daniel and I left Google, the thing we were sure about was the technology. We'd seen what these large language models could do internally, and it felt like the biggest thing that had ever happened in computing was sitting there not being shipped. So the first goal was just: get this into the hands of a lot of people and see what they do with it.

The way I thought about it was that you've got a technology that's really general. It can do a lot of things, and it's hard to predict in advance which ones people will actually want. So rather than guessing, you build something open-ended and let users tell you. The character framing came out of that. If you let someone define who they're talking to, you've essentially let them build the product themselves. Some people wanted a tutor, some people wanted to practice a job interview, some people wanted a friend to talk to at two in the morning, some people wanted to roleplay a story. We didn't have to pick.

And what we found pretty quickly was that the entertainment and companionship use cases were enormous, way bigger than I'd have guessed sitting at Google thinking about search and productivity. People were spending hours a day. That told us something about what the technology was good for right now, as opposed to what it might be good for once it stopped making things up. For a lot of these uses, a model that's occasionally wrong or a little strange isn't a bug. It's fine. Whereas if you're trying to replace a doctor, it's a problem.

So the product philosophy became: build the model, build the infrastructure to serve it cheaply at scale, give people maximal freedom to shape the experience, and pay attention to where the engagement goes. The users were a lot more creative than we were.

r001.rationale: It says the first goal was to put the technology in many people’s hands and see what they did with it.

r002.rationale: It connects entertainment and companionship use cases to models that make things up, explaining that occasional wrong or strange responses are acceptable in those settings rather than a bug.

astra-6.text:
We started with the idea that conversation itself could be the product. You have this technology that can play different roles, and we didn’t want to limit it to one assistant with one personality. We wanted people to be able to create the characters they wanted to talk to and share them with other people.

Some of that is entertainment, but it can also be learning something, practicing a conversation, or getting help thinking through an idea. Rather than deciding in advance which of those was the use case, the idea was to make it easy to create things and see what people found valuable.

r001.rationale: It says the team wanted to enable character creation and learn what people found valuable, but does not clearly state an initial broad release to discover how users would use Character.

r002.rationale: It mentions entertainment as one possible use, but does not connect that use to hallucinations being a feature.

sol-6.1.text:
We wanted to make something that a lot of people could use, and the most natural interface seemed to be conversation. You shouldn’t have to understand machine learning or figure out how to write a particular kind of prompt. You should just be able to talk to somebody.

And instead of deciding that there was one personality or one use case that everybody wanted, we let people create characters. Someone might want a tutor, someone might want help writing a story, and someone might just want an entertaining conversation. The idea was to give people a very general capability in a form that was easy to understand, and then learn from what they actually enjoyed doing with it.

r001.rationale: The response says they wanted a product many people could use and would learn from what users enjoyed doing with it, communicating a broad release to discover user behavior.

r002.rationale: The response mentions entertaining conversation but does not connect entertainment use to hallucinations being a feature.
